summary: The Eucharist (Greek eucharistia, thanksgiving) is the central Christian sacrament of bread and wine, known variously as the Lord's Supper, Holy Communion, the Mass, and the Divine Liturgy, in which Christians eat bread and drink wine in obedience to the command reported at the Last Supper, 'Do this in remembrance of me' (1 Corinthians 11:24-25). It is attested in the New Testament institution narratives and the Johannine discourse on eating the flesh and blood of Christ (John 6), and in the earliest post-apostolic texts (the Didache, Justin Martyr, Ignatius of Antioch). The traditions differ over how Christ is present in it and what the rite effects, and those differing accounts are recorded here as the attributed teachings of each tradition.
description:
The Eucharist is the rite in which Christians take bread and wine, give thanks over them, and eat and drink, understood across the traditions as a memorial, a communion, and (in most traditions) a sacrifice or the making-present of Christ's one sacrifice. Its scriptural warrant is the institution at the Last Supper, reported in four New Testament narratives that closely agree: Paul, writing that he 'received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you', records that Jesus 'took bread, and when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me', and over the cup 'This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me', adding that 'as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come' (1 Corinthians 11:23-26); the three Synoptic accounts (Matthew 26:26-28, Mark 14:22-24, Luke 22:19-20) give the same words of institution over the bread and the cup. The command 'Do this in remembrance of me' (Greek eis ten emen anamnesin), present in Paul and Luke, is taken across the traditions as the rite's dominical institution. The Gospel of John, which does not narrate the institution at the Supper, contains instead the discourse in which Jesus says 'I am the living bread which came down from heaven', that 'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you', and that 'my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed' (John 6:51, 53, 55); the traditions read this discourse in eucharistic terms to differing degrees.

The rite is attested very early. The Didache (chapters 9-10), an early church order, gives thanksgivings 'concerning the Eucharist' over the cup ('the holy vine of David') and over the broken bread, with the prayer that as the broken bread 'was scattered over the hills and, when gathered, became one', so the church might be gathered into God's kingdom, and it restricts participation to the baptized. Justin Martyr, in the First Apology (chapters 65-67, c. 155), describes the Sunday assembly, the president giving thanks over bread and a cup of water mixed with wine, the people's 'Amen', and the deacons' distribution, and reports the church's teaching that 'not as common bread and common drink do we receive these' but that 'the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word ... is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh', citing the apostolic memoirs for the words 'this is My body' and 'This is My blood'. Ignatius of Antioch, early in the second century, refers to the Eucharist as the medicine of immortality and calls it the flesh of Christ, language attributed to him.

The later traditions share the rite while differing over the mode of Christ's presence and the nature of the act, and these positions are recorded here as attributed teachings, not adjudicated. The Roman Catholic Church teaches transubstantiation, that the whole substance of the bread and wine is converted into the body and blood of Christ, defined at the Council of Trent (Thirteenth Session, 1551), which taught that in the sacrament Christ is contained 'truly, really, and substantially'. The Lutheran tradition, following Martin Luther, affirms the true presence of the body and blood 'in, with, and under' the bread and wine (a sacramental union) while rejecting transubstantiation. The Reformed tradition, following John Calvin, teaches a real but spiritual feeding on the body and blood of Christ, received by faith through the power of the Holy Spirit, who unites the believer to the ascended Christ (Institutes IV.17). The tradition associated with Huldrych Zwingli emphasizes the Supper as a memorial and a sign, a commemoration of Christ's death and a pledge of the believer's profession. Eastern Orthodoxy affirms that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ and treats the manner of the change as a mystery, generally declining to bind it to the scholastic metaphysics of substance and accident. This entry describes the rite and its shared scriptural and early institution, and reports the divergent later interpretations as the attributed positions of their respective traditions.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes the Eucharist and reports the divergent accounts of Christ's presence and the nature of the rite (Catholic transubstantiation; Lutheran sacramental union, 'in, with, and under'; Reformed spiritual or pneumatic feeding by faith per Calvin; Zwinglian memorialism; Orthodox mystery) strictly as the attributed teachings of each tradition, per neutrality principles #1, #2, and #4. The editor does not adjudicate which account is correct; that is the sensitive point of this entry, and it is handled by attribution throughout. The dispute over the mode of presence has its own entry, real-presence, and the Catholic account its own, transubstantiation; this entry situates both within the shared rite.

Sourcing triangulates the three lenses per neutrality #8 as adapted for Christianity. (a) Academic historians of doctrine: Jaroslav Pelikan, The Christian Tradition, volumes 1 and 3 (University of Chicago Press), and Edward J. Kilmartin, The Eucharist in the West (Liturgical Press, 1998). (b) The primary corpus, read directly and open where possible: 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 and John 6:51-56 (biblehub, KJV); the Didache 9-10 (CCEL, Richardson); Justin Martyr, First Apology 65-67 (newadvent); the Council of Trent, Thirteenth Session (papalencyclicals); and Calvin, Institutes IV.17 (CCEL). (c) A contemporary Christian theologian on-topic: Alexander Schmemann, The Eucharist: Sacrament of the Kingdom (St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1988). No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY. Rated high, open primaries read line-by-line to confirm the exact cited wording: (1) 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, verified verbatim in the KJV at biblehub, including 'this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me', 'This cup is the new testament in my blood', and 'ye do shew the Lord's death till he come'; (2) John 6:51, 53, 55, 56, verified verbatim at biblehub; (3) the Didache 9-10, read at CCEL, the thanksgivings over the cup ('the holy vine of David'), the broken bread ('scattered ... and gathered'), and the restriction to the baptized confirmed; (4) Justin Martyr, First Apology 66, read directly at newadvent, the clause 'not as common bread and common drink' and 'the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word ... is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh' and the words 'this is My body' / 'This is My blood' confirmed verbatim; (5) the Council of Trent, Thirteenth Session, Canon I ('truly, really, and substantially ... the whole Christ') read directly at papalencyclicals; (6) Calvin, Institutes IV.17, read directly at CCEL, the chapter opening on the sacred Supper of the Lord, its refutation of transubstantiation, and its teaching of a spiritual feeding confirmed. Rated medium, verified to exist and be on-topic (via publisher and library catalogues and reviews) but not read line-by-line: Pelikan, Kilmartin, Schmemann, and the reference to Ignatius of Antioch. The Synoptic institution narratives (Matthew 26:26-28, Mark 14:22-24, Luke 22:19-20) are standard and are cited alongside 1 Corinthians 11; the Pauline and Johannine texts were the ones read verbatim here.

relations.note: The doctrine of the real presence, that Christ is genuinely present in the eucharistic elements, and the family of disagreements over the mode of that presence, is the contested question that arises within eucharistic theology; treated in its own entry. Created together with this entry.

Transubstantiation is the Roman Catholic account of what happens to the bread and wine in the Eucharist, defined at the Council of Trent; recorded as the attributed Catholic teaching within the shared rite, not adjudicated.

The Eucharist is one of the sacraments (one of the seven in the Catholic and Orthodox reckoning, one of two commonly retained in the Reformation traditions); situated within the tradition's sacramental theology.

The Council of Trent (Thirteenth Session, 1551) defined the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist and the real presence 'truly, really, and substantially', read directly at papalencyclicals. Attributed to the Catholic Church, not endorsed.

Calvin taught a real but spiritual feeding on the body and blood of Christ, received by faith through the Holy Spirit (Institutes IV.17, read directly at CCEL). Attributed to Calvin as the Reformed account, not adjudicated.
Luther affirmed the true presence of the body and blood 'in, with, and under' the bread and wine (a sacramental union) while rejecting transubstantiation. Attributed to Luther, not adjudicated.
Zwingli emphasized the Supper as a memorial and a sign, a commemoration of Christ's death and a pledge of profession. Attributed to Zwingli, not adjudicated.

In Roman Catholic theology the Eucharist (the Mass) is the sacrifice and sacrament in which, by transubstantiation, Christ is present truly, really, and substantially. Attributed to the Catholic Church, not endorsed.

Eastern Orthodoxy affirms that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ in the Divine Liturgy and treats the manner of the change as a mystery, generally declining the scholastic substance-and-accident metaphysics. Attributed to the Orthodox tradition, not adjudicated.

The Reformed tradition, following Calvin, holds a real but spiritual reception of Christ by faith through the Holy Spirit rather than a change of the substance of the elements. Attributed, not ranked.

historical_period.note: The rite is traced to the Last Supper (conventionally c. 30) and the words of institution reported in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 and the Synoptics; attested in the earliest post-apostolic texts (the Didache and Justin Martyr, mid-second century) and continuous in Christian worship to the present. No end date is asserted; the start marks the reported institution, and the divergent doctrinal accounts of the presence developed chiefly from the ninth century (the Carolingian debates) through the Reformation and Trent (1551).

sources.citation: The Holy Bible, 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 (KJV): Paul 'received of the Lord' the account that Jesus 'took bread, and when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me', and over the cup 'This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me', adding 'For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.' The earliest written institution narrative; the primary-corpus lens for the words of institution and the command 'Do this in remembrance of me'.
sources.license: Underlying Greek text public domain; KJV public domain. Verses 23-26 read directly, line-by-line (2026-07-26), and confirmed verbatim.

sources.citation: The Holy Bible, John 6:51, 53, 55, 56 (KJV): 'I am the living bread which came down from heaven'; 'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you'; 'For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed'; 'He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him.' The eucharistic discourse read across the traditions to differing degrees; the primary-corpus lens for the Johannine material.
sources.license: Underlying Greek text public domain; KJV public domain. Verses 51, 53, 55, 56 read directly, line-by-line (2026-07-26), and confirmed verbatim.

sources.citation: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), chapters 9-10, Richardson translation. Thanksgivings 'concerning the Eucharist': first over the cup ('for the holy vine of David') and then over the broken bread, with the prayer that as the broken bread 'was scattered over the hills and, when gathered, became one', so the church be gathered into God's kingdom; participation restricted to the baptized; chapter 10 gives the thanksgiving after the meal. Early church order; the primary-corpus lens for the earliest eucharistic prayers.
sources.license: Public-domain translation. Chapters 9-10 read directly, line-by-line, at the Christian Classics Ethereal Library (CCEL) (2026-07-26) and confirmed.

sources.citation: Justin Martyr, First Apology, chapters 65-67 (c. 155). Chapter 65 describes the assembly, the bread and cup, the president's thanksgiving, the people's 'Amen', and the deacons' distribution; chapter 66 teaches that 'not as common bread and common drink do we receive these' but that 'the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word ... is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh', citing the apostolic memoirs for 'this is My body' and 'This is My blood'; chapter 67 describes the Sunday assembly. Primary-corpus lens for the earliest full description of the rite.
sources.license: Public-domain translation (Ante-Nicene Fathers). Chapter 66 read directly, line-by-line (2026-07-26), and the cited clauses confirmed verbatim; chapters 65 and 67 confirmed on-topic.

sources.citation: The Council of Trent, Decree Concerning the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist (Thirteenth Session, 11 October 1551), Canon I: 'If any one denieth, that, in the sacrament of the most holy Eucharist, are contained truly, really, and substantially, the body and blood together with the soul and divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and consequently the whole Christ ... let him be anathema.' The primary-corpus lens for the Catholic definition of the real presence and (chapter IV, canon II) of transubstantiation.
sources.license: Underlying conciliar text public domain. Canon I read directly, line-by-line (2026-07-26), and confirmed verbatim.

sources.citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book IV, chapter 17 (Of the Lord's Supper, and the benefits conferred by it), Beveridge translation. Calvin refutes transubstantiation and teaches a real but spiritual feeding on the body and blood of Christ, received by faith through the secret power of the Holy Spirit, who truly unites the believer to the flesh and blood of the ascended Christ. The primary-corpus lens for the Reformed account.
sources.license: Public-domain translation. Chapter IV.17 read directly at CCEL (2026-07-26); the opening on the sacred Supper, the refutation of transubstantiation, and the teaching of a spiritual feeding confirmed.

sources.citation: Pelikan, Jaroslav. The Christian Tradition: A History of the Development of Doctrine. Volume 1, The Emergence of the Catholic Tradition (100-600), and Volume 3, The Growth of Medieval Theology (600-1300). Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1971, 1978. Standard scholarly history of the development of eucharistic doctrine, including the patristic testimony and the Carolingian and eleventh-century (Berengar) debates; the academic-historian lens.
